--- title: "Checking a fit" description: "How to tell whether the optimisation actually worked: the warnings that matter, the ones that do not, and the signatures of silent failure." order: 6 categories: [optimisation, reproducibility] --- ## Failure leaves signatures Everything so far in this section has described fitting as a search. A search can fail, and the useful thing about failure is that it leaves signatures. This page is about recognising them. The reason to care is that a failed fit does not usually look like a failed fit. It returns coefficients. It prints a summary. It makes predictions. A classifier for a rare species can produce a perfectly respectable ROC AUC while predicting presence at zero stations, with the optimisation working exactly as instructed ([class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd) shows why), which is precisely why you cannot rely on output looking reasonable. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea Three things can go wrong between asking for a fit and getting one: 1. **The search did not finish.** It ran out of iterations and returned wherever it had reached. 2. **The search finished somewhere arbitrary.** The objective had several minima and the starting point chose between them. 3. **The search finished nowhere.** The objective has no minimum in the direction the algorithm was heading, and it kept going until a limit stopped it. Each has a recognisable fingerprint, and all three are demonstrated below on this survey. ## Worked example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> select(abundance, present, catch_weight_kg, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season) |> drop_na() ``` ::: ### Failure 1: the search did not finish Iterative fits stop either because they converged or because they hit a cap. These are completely different outcomes and the printed coefficients look the same. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stopped_early <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m, data = d, family = binomial, control = glm.control(maxit = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} full_fit <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m, data = d, family = binomial) tibble( fit = c("maxit = 2", "run to convergence"), converged = c(stopped_early$converged, full_fit$converged), iterations = c(stopped_early$iter, full_fit$iter), chlorophyll = c(coef(stopped_early)[2], coef(full_fit)[2]), depth = c(coef(stopped_early)[3], coef(full_fit)[3]) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|fit |converged | iterations| chlorophyll| depth| |:------------------|:---------|----------:|-----------:|------:| |maxit = 2 |FALSE | 2| -0.3118| 0.0038| |run to convergence |TRUE | 5| -0.3442| 0.0037|
::: ::: The truncated fit reports a chlorophyll coefficient of −0.312 against the correct −0.344: 9% out, and entirely plausible-looking on its own. The only thing distinguishing them is `$converged`, which is a field you have to ask for. The habit worth forming: **after any iterative fit, check the convergence flag rather than the coefficients.** For `glm()` it is `fit$converged`. For `glm.nb()` it is a warning. For `nnet` and `glmnet` it is in the object. Under tidymodels, `extract_fit_engine()` gets you to it. ### Failure 2: the search finished nowhere This one produces the most memorable output in applied statistics. `catch_weight_kg` is the leaked column from [section 2](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd), computed from `abundance`, so it separates present from absent almost perfectly. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} separated <- glm(present ~ catch_weight_kg, data = d, family = binomial) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(summary(separated)$coefficients, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) #> (Intercept) 27.716 3074.802 0.009 0.993 #> catch_weight_kg -157.709 13515.391 -0.012 0.991 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(converged = separated$converged, iterations = separated$iter) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> converged iterations #> 0 25 ``` ::: ::: A coefficient of −157.7 with a standard error of 13,515 and a *p*-value of 0.99. Read that plainly: the model has found a predictor that classifies the response essentially perfectly, and reports it as the least significant variable you have ever seen. Both numbers are correct and neither is meaningful. When one predictor separates the classes, the likelihood has no maximum: pushing the coefficient further from zero always makes the data slightly more probable, forever. The algorithm walks off in that direction until it hits its iteration cap at 25, and the standard error, being the curvature of a surface that is flattening out towards infinity, goes to infinity with it. ::: {.callout-warning} **A gigantic coefficient with a gigantic standard error is not weak evidence. It is a separation warning.** The clue is the ratio: an estimate of 158 with an error of 13,515 is not an estimate at all. If you see this, look for a predictor that encodes the answer, which in real work usually means [leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd), as it does here. R does print `fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred`, and it is one of the few warnings that always means something. ::: ### Failure 3: the search finished somewhere arbitrary Not every algorithm lands in the same place twice. Random forests choose bootstrap samples and variable subsets at random, so an unseeded fit is a different model each time. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) split <- initial_split(d |> select(-present, -catch_weight_kg), prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) unseeded <- map_dbl(1:5, \(i) { forest <- ranger(abundance ~ ., data = train, num.trees = 500) sqrt(mean((test$abundance - predict(forest, test)$predictions)^2)) }) round(unseeded, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 4.7568 4.7398 4.7411 4.7305 4.7203 ``` ::: ::: Five runs, five answers, spanning 0.037 RMSE. That is small, and it is the point. Section 3's [comparison of its seven models](../03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd) found its two count models closer than that on the test sites, which is exactly why that page would not rank them on one split. **Run-to-run noise is a measurement you can make, and it sets the resolution of every comparison you go on to draw.** For k-means the same instability is much larger, because the objective genuinely has multiple minima: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- scale(d |> select(depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu)) single_starts <- map_dbl(1:20, \(i) kmeans(X, centers = 5, nstart = 1, iter.max = 50)$tot.withinss) tibble( `distinct solutions found` = n_distinct(round(single_starts, 3)), best = min(single_starts), worst = max(single_starts), `with nstart = 25` = kmeans(X, centers = 5, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| distinct solutions found| best| worst| with nstart = 25| |------------------------:|------:|------:|----------------:| | 10| 1093.8| 1151.2| 1093.8|
::: ::: Twenty runs of the same algorithm on the same data found ten different answers, the worst 5% worse than the best. Every one of them converged. This is the difference between the convex objectives of [regression](parameter-estimation.qmd), with one minimum always found, and objectives that are merely bumpy, and it is why [section 8](../08-unsupervised-learning/index.qmd) insists on `nstart`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 <- tibble(value = unseeded) |> ggplot(aes(value, 0)) + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "Test RMSE (individuals)", y = NULL, title = "Random forest, 5 unseeded runs") + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) p2 <- tibble(value = single_starts) |> ggplot(aes(value, 0)) + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + annotate("point", x = min(single_starts), y = 0, shape = 1, size = 6, stroke = 1, colour = "black") + labs(x = "Total within-cluster sum of squares", y = NULL, title = "k-means, 20 single random starts", subtitle = "Circled: the value nstart = 25 also finds") + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) p1 / p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Run-to-run variation from two algorithms with no seed set. The random forest's test RMSE varies over a narrow band; k-means' objective across twenty single random starts takes ten distinct values spanning 5%. Both algorithms reported success every time.](reading-a-fit_files/figure-html/fig-instability-1.png){#fig-instability fig-alt='Two panels of dot strips. The upper panel shows five random-forest test RMSE values clustered between 4.72 and 4.76, a span of under 0.04. The lower panel shows twenty k-means objective values scattered between 1094 and 1152, clumping at several distinct levels rather than spreading evenly, with a marked point at the lowest value labelled as the solution found with twenty-five restarts.' width=1400} ::: ::: ## Three failures, three responses The three failures need three different responses. | Signature | What happened | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | `converged = FALSE`, or a `maxit` warning | Ran out of iterations | Raise the cap; if it still fails, the model is wrong for the data | | Huge coefficient, huge standard error, *p* ≈ 1 | Separation: no maximum exists | Find the predictor that encodes the answer; suspect leakage | | Different answer each run | Stochastic algorithm, possibly multiple minima | Set a seed for reproducibility; measure the spread to know your resolution | | `NaN` loss, or coefficients exploding | Learning rate above the stable limit | Lower it; [scale the predictors](gradient-descent.qmd) | | Coefficients change wildly on small data changes | Flat valley, near-collinearity | Check correlations; consider [a prior](map-and-priors.qmd) | Two of these deserve emphasis because they are routinely misread. **Setting a seed makes a fit reproducible. It does not make it stable.** A seeded random forest returns the same number every time, which is necessary for a reproducible paper and tells you nothing about whether that number is reliable. The way to find out is to remove the seed deliberately and run it several times, as above. Reproducibility and stability are different properties and only one of them is about your science. **Warnings are not all equal.** `fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred` always means something. So does `algorithm did not converge`. By contrast, the rank-deficiency and `NA` coefficients that `lm()` produces from collinear predictors arrive with no warning at all: R simply drops a term and prints `NA` in the table, and nothing tells you it happened. The loud messages are not a reliable guide to the dangerous failures. ### A checklist After fitting any model in this course, before reading a single coefficient: 1. Did it converge? Not "did it print output": check the flag. 2. Are any coefficients absurd in size, or are any `NA`? 3. Is any standard error orders of magnitude larger than its estimate? 4. If the algorithm is stochastic, what does it do on a second run without a seed? 5. Are the predictions in a possible range, with no negative counts, no probabilities outside (0, 1), nothing outside what the species can do? Item 5 catches more real mistakes than the other four combined, and it needs no statistics at all. ## Limits of these checks **A converged fit can still be the wrong model.** Everything on this page is about whether the optimisation did what it was asked. It cannot tell you whether you asked for the right thing. A Poisson model on overdispersed counts converges beautifully; [section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) is about that second question. **Convergence tolerances are set by package authors, not by you.** "Converged" means "changed by less than some default on the last iteration", and defaults vary between packages fitting the same model. Two packages can disagree in the third decimal and both report success. **Some failures have no signature at all.** Section 2's [stratified split](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) silently ignored the stratification variable, produced a worse balance than not stratifying, and issued no warning of any kind. No checklist would have caught it. Only checking that the result was what you asked for did. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Check the **convergence flag**, not the plausibility of the coefficients. A fit stopped after two iterations here was 9% out and looked entirely normal. - A huge coefficient with a huge standard error and *p* ≈ 1 means **separation**, not weak evidence: here, a coefficient of −158 with an error of 13,515 from a leaked predictor. - Stochastic algorithms give a different answer per run: the forest varied by 0.037 RMSE, k-means found ten distinct solutions out of twenty runs. - **Seeding gives reproducibility, not stability.** Remove the seed on purpose to measure how much your result moves, and treat that spread as the resolution of your comparisons. - The warnings that print loudest are not the failures most likely to mislead you. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Fit `glm(present ~ abundance, family = binomial)` on this data. `present` is defined as `abundance > 0`, so the separation is exact. Compare the coefficient and standard error to the `catch_weight_kg` version: which is worse, and why does that ordering make sense? 2. Run the k-means block with `centers = 2` instead of 5. Does the number of distinct solutions go up or down, and what does that suggest about the relationship between model complexity and the number of places an algorithm can get stuck?
